questions.q: Why do rational arguments fail once emotions take over a negotiation?
a: The emotional side must be addressed before facts can land
People forget the facts when they feel under pressure
Rational points take too long to explain clearly
Facts usually favor whichever side prepared more
questions.why: Lesson 1 says every negotiation has a factual and an emotional side that cannot be separated.

questions.q: What should you do before agreeing to a solution?
a: Talk through every option, including extreme ones
Decide on your preferred outcome in advance
Let the more experienced side propose terms
Narrow the discussion to two realistic choices
questions.why: Lesson 2 recommends listing all potential solutions first, then choosing what meets both sides' needs.

questions.q: Why does fixating on one solution hurt a negotiation?
a: It ignores what the other person actually needs
It makes the conversation take much longer
It gives the other side too much information
It hides your real priorities from them
questions.why: Lesson 2 says starting from a fixed solution only looks at one side of the problem.

questions.q: What should you learn about before a negotiation?
a: The other person's values, goals and interests
The market rate for the goods involved
The other side's weaknesses and past failures
The exact wording of the contract
questions.why: Lesson 3 says preparation means understanding the people and context, including their values and goals.

questions.q: What does the summary say happens if you enter a negotiation unprepared?
a: You waste time arguing over emotions and assumptions
You are forced to accept the first offer made
You lose the chance to brainstorm any options
You appear far less confident than the other side
questions.why: Lesson 3 warns that without preparation you will argue over unforeseen emotions and prejudices.
